usamo-usajmo-2022-01.title: Look at three consecutive terms
usamo-usajmo-2022-01.body:
Let $(x_k)_{k\ge0}$ be an arithmetic progression with difference $d$, $x_k = s + kd$, which is also geometric: $x_{k+1} = r\,x_k$ for some $r$ and all $k$. Then $x_{k+1}^2 = r^2x_k^2 = x_k x_{k+2}$, i.e. for three consecutive terms $s - d, s, s+d$:
$$s^2 \equiv (s-d)(s+d) = s^2 - d^2 \pmod m, \quad\text{so}\quad d^2 \equiv 0 \pmod m.$$

**If $m$ is squarefree:** every prime $p \mid m$ divides $d^2$, hence $d$; so $m \mid d$ and the progression is constant. No nonconstant example exists (this includes $m = 1$).

**If $p^2 \mid m$ for a prime $p$:** let $d = m/p$, so $0 < d < m$ and $d^2 = m \cdot \frac{m}{p^2} \equiv 0 \pmod m$. Take $x_k = 1 + kd$ and $r = 1 + d$. Then
$$r x_k = (1+d)(1+kd) = 1 + (k+1)d + kd^2 \equiv 1 + (k+1)d = x_{k+1} \pmod m,$$
so the sequence is geometric, arithmetic, and nonconstant ($x_1 - x_0 = d \not\equiv 0$).

**Answer:** exactly the positive integers $m$ that are not squarefree. ∎

usamo-usajmo-2022-02.title: Averaging plus a discrete intermediate value argument
usamo-usajmo-2022-02.body:
Let $N = a + b + 1$. A **transversal** is a set of $N$ cells, one in each row and each column (it corresponds to a permutation $\sigma$ of the columns: cells $(i, \sigma(i))$).

**Step 1.** For a uniformly random transversal, each cell is included with probability $\frac1N$. So the expected number of amber cells is at least
$$\frac{a^2 + ab - b}{a + b + 1} = (a - 1) + \frac{1}{a+b+1} > a - 1,$$
since $(a-1)(a+b+1) = a^2 + ab - b - 1$. Hence some transversal $T_1$ has at least $a$ amber cells. By the same computation for bronze, some transversal $T_2$ has at least $b$ bronze cells, i.e. at most $N - b = a + 1$ amber cells.

**Step 2.** Every permutation is a product of transpositions, so we can go from $T_1$ to $T_2$ by a sequence of transversals in which consecutive ones differ by swapping the columns of two rows: cells $(i, \sigma(i)), (j, \sigma(j))$ are replaced by $(i, \sigma(j)), (j, \sigma(i))$. Each such step changes the number of amber cells by at most $2$.

The amber count starts at a value $\ge a$ and ends at a value $\le a+1$. If it starts at $a$ or $a+1$ we are done. Otherwise it starts $\ge a+2$; consider the first transversal in the sequence with count $\le a+1$. The previous one has count $\ge a+2$, and they differ by at most $2$, so this one has count $\ge a$, i.e. count $a$ or $a+1$.

**Step 3.** A transversal with exactly $a$ amber cells has $b+1$ bronze cells; one with $a+1$ amber cells has $b$ bronze cells. In either case choose $a$ amber and $b$ bronze cells from it; they lie in distinct rows and columns. ∎

usamo-usajmo-2022-03.title: Swap two adjacent colors
usamo-usajmo-2022-03.body:
Let the sides of the $2n$-gon, traversed counterclockwise, be the unit vectors $e_0, e_1, \dots, e_{2n-1}$, where $e_k$ makes angle $\frac{k\pi}{n}$ with $e_0$; so $e_{k+n} = -e_k$ and sides $k$ and $k+n$ are parallel. A coloring is a choice of color for each direction class $k \bmod n$. The polygon $B$ is the convex polygon whose sides are the black vectors in increasing angular order, and similarly for $W$. Write $p \times q$ for the cross product $p_xq_y - p_yq_x$.

Any two colorings with $b$ black classes can be transformed into each other by repeatedly swapping the colors of two **adjacent** classes $k$ and $k+1$ of different colors. So it suffices to show such a swap does not change $[B] - [W]$.

Suppose class $k$ is black and class $k+1$ is white; let $u = e_k$, $v = e_{k+1}$. Let $x$ be the sum of the black vectors $e_j$ with $k+2 \le j \le k+n-1$, and $y$ the sum of the white ones in the same range. Before the swap, the sides of $B$ in order are: $u$, then the black vectors summing to $x$, then $-u$, then their negatives summing to $-x$. Draw the parallelogram with sides $u$ and $x$ inside $B$: it splits $B$ into this parallelogram and two congruent (centrally symmetric) pieces bounded by the chain summing to $x$ and its chord. If $q_B$ is the area of one piece, then
$$[B_{\text{before}}] = u \times x + 2q_B, \qquad [B_{\text{after}}] = v\times x + 2q_B,$$
since after the swap $B$ has the same chain with $u$ replaced by $v$ (and $-u$ by $-v$). Here all cross products are positive because the vectors in $x$ have angles strictly between those of $v$ and $v + \pi$ (hence also of $u$ and $u+\pi$). Similarly, with $q_W$ the area of the piece of $W$ cut off by the chain summing to $y$,
$$[W_{\text{before}}] = v \times y + 2q_W, \qquad [W_{\text{after}}] = u \times y + 2q_W .$$
So the difference $[B] - [W]$ is unchanged iff
$$u\times x - v \times y = v \times x - u \times y \iff (u - v)\times(x + y) = 0,$$
i.e. iff $u - v$ and $x + y$ are parallel.

**Claim.** Both $u - v$ and $x + y$ are perpendicular to $u + v$.

*Proof.* $(u - v)\cdot(u + v) = |u|^2 - |v|^2 = 0$. For the other: $u + v + x + y = e_k + e_{k+1} + \dots + e_{k+n-1}$ is the sum of $n$ consecutive sides, i.e. the vector from a vertex $P$ of the $2n$-gon to the diametrically opposite vertex $P'$. The point $Q = P + u + v$ is also a vertex, hence on the circle with diameter $PP'$, so by Thales $\angle PQP' = 90^\circ$: $(u + v) \perp (x + y)$. $\square$

In the plane, two vectors perpendicular to the same nonzero vector are parallel. Hence the swap preserves $[B] - [W]$, which therefore depends only on $b$ and $w$. ∎

usamo-usajmo-2022-03.title: Compute the difference exactly
usamo-usajmo-2022-03.body:
With the notation $e_k$ as above, the area of a convex polygon with consecutive side vectors $v_1, \dots, v_m$ (counterclockwise) is $\frac12\sum_{i<j} v_i \times v_j$. Let $\varepsilon_k = +1$ if class $k \bmod n$ is black and $-1$ if white, and $s_{ij} = e_i\times e_j = \sin\frac{(j-i)\pi}n$. Using $\mathbf 1_{\text{black}} = \frac{1+\varepsilon}2$, $\mathbf 1_{\text{white}} = \frac{1-\varepsilon}2$,
$$[B] - [W] = \frac12\sum_{0\le i<j\le 2n-1}\left(\tfrac{(1+\varepsilon_i)(1+\varepsilon_j)}{4} - \tfrac{(1-\varepsilon_i)(1-\varepsilon_j)}4\right)s_{ij} = \frac14\sum_{i<j}(\varepsilon_i + \varepsilon_j)s_{ij},$$
which is *linear* in the $\varepsilon$'s: $[B]-[W] = \frac14\sum_i \varepsilon_i c_i$ with $c_i = \sum_{j \ne i}\sin\frac{|j-i|\pi}{n}$. Using $\sum_{d=1}^{2n-1}\sin\frac{d\pi}{n} = 0$ one finds $c_i = 2\sum_{d=1}^{i}\sin\frac{d\pi}n$, and then, with $\omega = e^{i\pi/n}$, $c_i + c_{i+n} = 2\operatorname{Im}\frac{2\omega}{1-\omega} = 2\cot\frac{\pi}{2n}$ for every $i$. Since $\varepsilon_{i+n} = \varepsilon_i$,
$$[B] - [W] = \frac14\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon_i\,(c_i + c_{i+n}) = \frac{b - w}{2}\cot\frac{\pi}{2n},$$
which depends only on $b$ and $w$. (Check: with $w = 0$ this is the area $\frac n2\cot\frac{\pi}{2n}$ of the regular $2n$-gon of side $1$.) ∎

usamo-usajmo-2022-04.title: Translation, then coordinates
usamo-usajmo-2022-04.body:
**Step 1: $L = K + \vec{AD}$.** Let $t = \vec{AD} = \vec{BC}$ and $K' = K + t$. The translation by $t$ maps $A \mapsto D$, $B \mapsto C$, so $K'D = KA$ and $K'C = KB$. Thus $K'$ and $L$ are both points on the perpendicular bisector of $CD$ at distance $r = KA$ from $C$ and $D$; there are exactly two such points, mirror images in line $CD$.

The rhombus lies between the parallel lines $AB$ and $DC$, and $t$ moves line $AB$ onto line $DC$. Since $K$ is strictly between these lines, $K'$ lies strictly on the far side of $DC$ (outside the rhombus), at distance $h = \operatorname{dist}(K, AB)$ from $DC$. The other candidate is the point on the perpendicular bisector of $CD$ at distance $h$ from $CD$ on the rhombus side, which is the reflection $K^*$ of $K$ through the center $O$ of the rhombus (the half-turn about $O$ swaps $AB$ and $CD$). $K^*$ is inside the rhombus, while $L$ is outside; so $L = K'$.

**Step 2: coordinates.** Put $O$ at the origin with the diagonals on the axes: $A = (-p, 0)$, $B = (0, -q)$, $C = (p, 0)$, $D = (0, q)$, so $t = D - A = (p, q)$, and write $K = (k_1, k_2)$, $L = (k_1 + p, k_2 + q)$. The condition $KA = KB$ reads
$$(k_1 + p)^2 + k_2^2 = k_1^2 + (k_2 + q)^2 \iff q k_2 - p k_1 = \tfrac{p^2 - q^2}{2}. \tag{$*$}$$

Let $G = \frac{K + L}2 = \left(k_1 + \frac p2,\ k_2 + \frac q2\right)$ and choose
$$X = (2G_x, 0) \in AC, \qquad Y = (0, 2G_y) \in BD.$$
Then $XY$ and $KL$ have the same midpoint $G$, so $KXLY$ is a parallelogram. It is a rhombus iff its diagonals are perpendicular: $\vec{XY} = (-2G_x, 2G_y)$ and $\vec{KL} = (p, q)$, so we need $-pG_x + qG_y = 0$, i.e.
$$q\left(k_2 + \tfrac q2\right) = p\left(k_1 + \tfrac p2\right) \iff qk_2 - pk_1 = \tfrac{p^2 - q^2}2,$$
which is exactly $(*)$.

Finally it is non-degenerate: $K \ne L$, and $X = Y$ would force $G = O$, i.e. $K = -\frac t2$, the midpoint of $AB$, which is not inside the rhombus. ∎

usamo-usajmo-2022-05.title: Difference of squares
usamo-usajmo-2022-05.body:
$(3, 2)$ works: $3 - 2 = 1$ and $6 - 2 = 4$. We show it is the only pair.

If $p = q$, then $pq - q = q(q-1)$ is a product of two coprime consecutive positive integers, so both would be squares; but the prime $q$ is not a square. If $p < q$ then $p - q < 0$. So $p > q$. Write
$$a^2 = p - q, \qquad b^2 = pq - q = q(p-1),$$
with $a, b$ positive integers.

- $a^2 = p - q < p$, so $a < p$.
- $b^2 = q(p-1) \le (p-1)^2 < p^2$, so $b < p$.
- $b^2 - a^2 = pq - p = p(q - 1) > 0$, so $b > a$.

Hence $(b - a)(b + a) = p(q-1)$ with $0 < b - a < p$, so the prime $p$ does not divide $b - a$ and must divide $b + a$. As $0 < b + a < 2p$, we get $b + a = p$ and therefore $b - a = q - 1$.

Adding, $2b = p + q - 1$, so $p + q$ is odd and one of $p, q$ equals $2$; since $q < p$, $q = 2$. Then $b - a = 1$ and $b + a = p$ give $a = \frac{p-1}2$, and $a^2 = p - 2$ becomes
$$(p-1)^2 = 4(p - 2) \iff p^2 - 6p + 9 = 0 \iff p = 3.$$

**Answer:** $(p, q) = (3, 2)$. ∎

usamo-usajmo-2022-05.title: Divisibility
usamo-usajmo-2022-05.body:
As above $p > q$. Since $q(p-1)$ is a square and $q$ is prime, $q \mid p - 1$ and $\frac{p-1}{q}$ is a square. Then
$$s^2 := (p - q)\cdot\frac{p-1}{q}$$
is a square, and solving for $q$ gives $q = \dfrac{p^2 - p}{s^2 + p - 1}$. So $s^2 + p - 1$ divides $p(p-1)$, and in particular $s < p$.

- If $p \nmid s^2 + p - 1$, then $s^2 + p - 1 \mid p - 1$, forcing $s = 0$, i.e. $p = q$, already excluded.
- If $p \mid s^2 + p - 1$, then $s^2 \equiv 1 \pmod p$, so $s = 1$ or $s = p - 1$. If $s = p-1$ then $q = \frac{p(p-1)}{p(p-1)} = 1$, not prime. If $s = 1$ then $q = p - 1$, so $q = 2$, $p = 3$. ∎

usamo-usajmo-2022-06.title: A miraculous identity
usamo-usajmo-2022-06.body:
Let $s_n = |a_n|^2 + |b_n|^2 + |c_n|^2$ and drop the index $n$ for the moment, writing $a, b, c$.

**Claim.** $s_{n+1} - s_n^2 = 2\left|a\bar b + b\bar c + c\bar a\right|^2$.

*Proof.* Using $|z|^2 = z\bar z$,
$$|a^2 + 2bc|^2 = |a|^4 + 2a^2\bar b\bar c + 2\bar a^2bc + 4|b|^2|c|^2,$$
and summing cyclically,
$$s_{n+1} = \sum|a|^4 + 4\sum|b|^2|c|^2 + 4\operatorname{Re}\left(\bar a^2bc + \bar b^2ca + \bar c^2ab\right).$$
Since $s_n^2 = \sum |a|^4 + 2\sum|b|^2|c|^2$,
$$s_{n+1} - s_n^2 = 2\sum|b|^2|c|^2 + 4\operatorname{Re}\left(\bar a^2bc + \bar b^2ca + \bar c^2ab\right).$$
On the other hand, for $X = a\bar b$, $Y = b\bar c$, $Z = c\bar a$,
$$|X + Y + Z|^2 = |X|^2 + |Y|^2 + |Z|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}(X\bar Y + Y\bar Z + Z\bar X),$$
where $|X|^2 + |Y|^2 + |Z|^2 = \sum|a|^2|b|^2$ and $X\bar Y = a\bar b\,\bar b c = \bar b^2 ca$, $Y\bar Z = \bar c^2 ab$, $Z\bar X = \bar a^2 bc$. Doubling gives exactly the expression above. $\square$

Hence $s_{n+1} \ge s_n^2$ for all $n$ (and all $s_n \ge 0$), so by induction
$$s_n \ge s_0^{2^n}.$$
If $s_0 > 1$, the right side tends to infinity, so $s_n$ is unbounded. But the hypothesis gives $s_n \le 3 \cdot 2022^2$ for all $n$. Therefore $s_0 \le 1$, i.e. $|a_0|^2 + |b_0|^2 + |c_0|^2 \le 1$. ∎

*Remark.* Another route: swap the names of $b_n, c_n$ in alternate steps so that $z_n = a_n + \omega b_n + \omega^2c_n$ ($\omega^3 = 1$) satisfies $z_{n+1} = z_n^2$.
